utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-96-23/2-S, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today we're here for sentencing hearing in the case against Mr. Zelenovic. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution is represented this morning by trial attorney Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky, case manager Ms. Vera Balikic, and my name is Christina Moeller, also a trial attorney in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Zoran Jovanovic, attorney at law, appearing for Mr. Dragan Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Zelenovic, can you hear us in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please be seated and be attentive on everything that we say. May I just start with verifying that both parties have not expressed any wish to call witnesses, and specifically that the Defence will not call the expert witness. We have received a report and -- but there is no need to further examine this expert witness. Is that correct, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence has submitted an expert report along with its brief, and we felt there was no need to call the expert as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's then well understood. I suggest to you that both parties will have an opportunity to further present their case as far as sentencing is concerned, that then perhaps the Judges might have some additional questions, that then after that the parties have a second round to make brief submissions, oral submissions, and that will then conclude this hearing. May I just try to find out, Ms. Moeller, at least if you are in charge, how much time would the Prosecution think it would need to -- not to repeat what we found already in the sentencing brief but to add or to clarify matters or perhaps to emphasise certain aspects of your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I would need probably 20, 25 minutes for a short statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jovanovic. How much time do you think you need? And I emphasise again that the Chamber is not that much interested in having everything repeated. I noticed that, for example, in your pre-sentencing brief that parts of the expert report are repeated almost literally. How much time would you need to briefly present your case in terms of sentencing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not longer than the Prosecution will take. I only wish to draw attention to some issues already mentioned in the brief, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's accepted, although, of course, the sentencing briefs are public documents, nevertheless, in a public hearing it's appropriate to draw attention to certain aspects of the case. Ms. Moeller, you have 25 minutes for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please the Court, on 14 December 2007, the accused entered into a plea agreement with the Prosecution pleading guilty to the crimes of torture and rape as crimes against humanity committed against Muslim women in the municipality of Foca in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. These crimes are punishable under Article 5(f) and 5(g) of the Statute of the Tribunal. On 17 January 2007, a hearing was held concerning this plea agreement where the accused pled guilty to seven counts of the amended indictment. Subsequently, the Trial Chamber found the accused guilty under three counts of torture and four counts of rape. The Prosecution then orally withdrew the remaining charges of the amended indictment. Mr. Dragan Zelenovic admitted that he committed torture and rape as a crime against humanity as a perpetrator and/or co-perpetrator in all but one cases. The one case for which he admitted aiding and abetting rape as a crime against humanity concerned the gang-rape of victim FWS-75, as contained in paragraph 5.4 of the amended indictment. Dragan Zelenovic admitted that the crimes he pled guilty to occurred in the context of the armed conflict and that they were part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population of Foca and its surrounding villages. He admitted that he had knowledge of the wider context in which he committed his crimes. Dragan Zelenovic is thus guilty by virtue of Articles 5(f) and (g) and Article 7(1) of the Statute. The purpose of the hearing today is to determine the appropriate sentence for this accused. Now, what is the appropriate sentence that should be meted out for the crimes committed by this accused? The case law of the Tribunal established -- yes. Sorry. I've been told to slow down, which I will try to. The case law of the Tribunal established four factors that the Trial Chamber must consider in sentencing. First, the gravity of the offence; second, the individual circumstances of the convicted person and the role he played in the commission of the crimes; third, are there any aggravating or mitigating circumstances; and fourth, the sentencing practices of the former Yugoslavia. I will now turn to the gravity of the offences. The Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case confirmed that the first factor, the gravity of the offence, is the primary consideration in imposing sentence. This finding has repeatedly been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber and followed by Trial Chambers. Thus the gravity of the offence is committed by Mr. Zelenovic must be the single most important factor to be considered by the Trial Chamber in determining his sentence. In determining the gravity, not only the general nature of the offence but also the individual circumstances and consequences of a crime must be considered. Factors that should be taken into account include the number of victims and the degree of suffering inflicted upon them by the accused. On the basis of the admissions of the accused, the following facts have been established: The city and municipality of Foca is located south-east of Sarajevo in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina bordering Serbia and Montenegro. According to a 1991 census Foca was a multi-ethnic city consisting of 52 per cent Muslims, 45 per cent Serbs, and 3 per cent others. On 8 April, 1992, first military actions started in the town of Foca. Serb forces started shelling the town with heavy artillery. The attack on Foca and its surrounding villages were part of an armed conflict that took place at that time throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina between forces of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serb forces. These Serb forced effected the removal of the majority of the non-Serb population from the municipality through violence. Muslim and other non-Serb civilians were subjected to widespread and systematic pattern of abuse. They were methodically rounded up and in the course of the capture were frequently brutalised, beaten, and sometimes even killed. Men, women, and children were separated and transported to different detention facilities. In the detention facilities civilians were subjected to humiliating and degrading conditions of life. Women and girls were frequently taken from these detention centres to be sexually assaulted and raped by Serb soldiers and policemen. The Accused Dragan Zelenovic, as a member of the Dragan Nikolic unit and the de facto military policemen in Foca, was one of the men who participated in the takeover of Foca municipality and the subsequent abuse of its non-Serb population. He, together with other soldiers, repeatedly took women and girls from various detention centres in order to rape and abuse them. These detention centres were established at Buk Bijela, Foca High School, and Partizan Sports Hall. On 3 July 1992, Dragan Zelenovic along with co-perpetrators arrested a group of about 60 Muslim women, children, and a few elderly men from Tosanj, and Mjesaja and took them to a detention facility called Buk Bijela. The Muslim civilians were interrogated on the hiding places of male villagers and the weapons. During one of these interrogations Dragan Zelenovic aided and abetted the gang-rape of victim FWS-75 who was raped by at least 10 soldiers on this occasion. During another interrogation he was one of four soldiers who gang-raped FWS-87. During this rape one of the soldiers threatened the victim by putting a gun to her head. Between 3 and about 13 July, 1992, about 70 Muslim inhabitants of Foca were detained in two classrooms at Foca High School, including those women, children, and elderly who had earlier been detained at Buk Bijela. The women were subjected to constant sexual assaults by Serb soldiers. Dragan Zelenovic was one of these soldiers. On or about 6 or 7 July, 1992, Dragan Zelenovic, in concert with other co-perpetrators, selected four women and girls from the classroom. Among them were again FWS-75 and FWS-87. Dragan Zelenovic led them to another classroom and decided which woman should go to which man. Then Zelenovic himself raped FWS-75 while the other men raped the other three victims. Between 8 and about 13 July 1992, Dragan Zelenovic together with other co-perpetrators took FWS-75 and FWS-87 out of Foca High School on several occasions. On one of these occasions Witness FWS-75 was subjected to a gang-rape in which he participated with three other soldiers. This rape took place in his own apartment in the Brena apartment block in Foca. On this same occasion, he also raped FWS-87. On two other occasions during this time he and several soldiers took FWS-75 and FWS-87 to other apartments in the Brena Block and raped them. Dragan Zelenovic raped both victims on this occasion. On yet another occasion during this time he took the two women to an abandoned house in Gornje Polje where he raped FWS-87. Dragan Zelenovic also took women and girls from Partizan Sports Hall in order to rape them. Partizan Sports Hall served as a detention facility from on or about 13 July until 13 August 1992. The detained women, children, and elderly held there numbered about 70. Living conditions for the detainees were brutal at this facility. They were subjected to inhumane treatment, lack of hygiene, overcrowding, starvations, and psychological and physical torture including constant sexual assaults. In July 1992, Dragan Zelenovic took victim FWS-87 who had been transferred to Partizan from Foca High School from the detention facility and gang-raped her along with three co-perpetrators. He assaulted FWS-87 once more on or about 30 October 1992. At this time, FWS-87, FWS-75, and other females were detained in a house known as Karaman's house. Dragan Zelenovic, together with three co-perpetrators, took FWS-87, FWS-75, and two other females from Karaman's house and brought them to an apartment near the fish restaurant in Foca. While the other co-perpetrators raped the other women, Zelenovic raped FWS-87. These women continued to be detained at different houses and apartments and continued to be subjected to sexual assaults by different groups of soldiers. The takeover of Foca town was complete by April 1992. The attack on the surrounding villages continued until mid-July 1992. After extended periods of detention, the non-Serb civilians were deported or forcibly transferred to Montenegro or locations controlled by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The remaining non-Serb population outside the detention centres was subjected to discriminatory measures including restriction of movements, searching of their homes, arbitrary beatings, killings, plunder, and destruction of homes and cultural and religious monuments that made their stay in Foca unbearable. The consequence of this widespread and systematic attack upon the non-Serb civilian population of Foca and its surroundings was that all traces of Muslim presence in the area were effectively wiped out, that nearly all Muslim civilians were expelled from the area. In 1994, Foca was renamed Srbinje, the Serb town, referring to the fact that it is now almost exclusively inhabited by Serbs. The Prosecution submits that the individual circumstances established, as well as the general nature of the offences committed by this accused must be considered to be of severe gravity. As the Prosecution submitted in its sentencing brief, a crime against humanity constitutes a crime which impacts beyond the immediate victims because it entails a widespread and/or systematic attack on a civilian population as one of its elements of crime, the perpetrator's conduct is concerned not only towards the immediate victim but towards the whole of humankind. As has been noted by the Trial Chamber in Prosecutor versus Erdemovic, when a crime against humanity is committed, "humanity comes under attack and is negated." The general nature of the specific underlying offences of rape and torture has also already been commented on by Chambers in the Tribunal. In Prosecutor versus Cesic it was held that rape must be considered a particularly serious offence because it violates the physical as well the physical integrity of the victims. It was also noted that rape is an inherently humiliating offence and that humiliation is to be taken into account when determining the gravity of a crime. The general nature and gravity of the particular offence of rape and torture was also addressed in the case Prosecutor versus Kunarac, Kovac, and Vukovic, which concerned three accused who received severe sentences for having committed crimes against female victims in Foca and its surrounding villages and who therefore are co-perpetrators of this accused. Presiding Judge Mumba in delivering the judgement in this case found through the sexual assaults and raped, and I quote, "Muslims, women and girls, mothers and daughters together were robbed of their last vestiges of human dignity. Women and girls treated like chattels, pieces of property, at the arbitrary disposal of the Serb occupation forces." Similarly the Trial Chamber in Prosecutor versus Furundzija, a case which also dealt with sexual violence committed in armed conflict held that torture by means of rape shall be considered a vicious form of torture. It is thus submitted that the gravity of the offences of rape and torture is such is that demands a substantial punishment. In addition to the general gravity of the offence, the Trial Chamber must take into account also the specific circumstances of each particular case including the form and degree of participation of the accused in the crimes. Mr. Zelenovic participated as a perpetrator, co-perpetrator, and in one case as aider and abettor in numerous rapes and tortures. He participated in the sexual assault of several women at Buk Bijela. He participated in the rape and sexual abuse of several women at Foca High School. He also did so repeatedly in an apartment building called Brena in the centre of Foca. He took a victim from Partizan Sports Hall and gang-raped her together with three other men. He took several women out of Karaman's house and raped one of them in an apartment near the fish restaurant in Foca. It is therefore established that the accused committed multiple rapes, many of which were gang-rapes in which the victims were assaulted by four and more men. One of these gang-rapes which he aided and abetted was so violent that the victim at some point lost consciousness. During another gang-rape in which he was a co-perpetrator, the victim was threatened with a gun to her head while being abused. The accused raped some of the victims in all possible ways and victim FWS-75 and FWS-87 were repeatedly assaulted by him while being transferred through different defence centres. At one occasion the accused hosted the gang-rape of FWS-75 by four soldiers including himself in his own apartment. On this occasion he also raped FWS-87. On yet another occasion it was the accused who determined who of four girls who had been taken out of Foca High School should go to which soldier to be raped. He over and again abused two particular victims, FWS-75 and FWS-87, in all possible ways. FWS-87 at the relevant time was a 15-year-old girl. Dragan Zelenovic showed no mercy for this child but abused her while she was transferred to the detention centres of Buk Bijela, Foca High School, and Partizan Sports Hall. After she was transferred from Partizan Sports Hall to Karaman's house he also found her there and took her out once more to abuse her. Dragan Zelenovic committed these offences against particularly vulnerable and defenseless women and children. He picked his victims on the grounds of ethnic and gender discrimination. He committed rape and torture over an extended period of time in relation to victims FWS-75 and FWS-87. More than one victim was involved in the commission of his offences. The gang-rapes he committed in concert with other perpetrators. By all these acts, Dragan Zelenovic showed the most glaring disrespect for the women's dignity and the fundamental human right to sexual self-determination. It was accepted that Dragan Zelenovic was not the mastermind behind the patterns of sexual assault committed against Muslim women and girls in the Foca area. It is accepted he had no command responsibility for particular authority over other soldiers and co-perpetrators. However, as his admissions show, his participation in the pattern of sexual assaults and terror was substantial. Another important factor to be considered when determining the gravity of an offence is the suffering inflicted upon the victims. Two victims who were repeatedly assaulted, as already mentioned, were FWS-75 and FWS-87. In 1992 FWS-75 was 25 years old. In July 1992, when her village was attacked, she was taken from Buk Bijela -- to Buk Bijela, then to Foca High School, taken out from there to different apartments, and further transferred to Partizan Sports Hall and from there onwards to other places. During her horrible odyssey, FWS-75 was constantly raped and sexually assaulted. Dragan Zelenovic was not the only soldier who abused her but one among others. As already mentioned, FWS-87 was only 15 years old in 1992, and she was forced on a similar odyssey during which time she was transferred from detention centre to detention centre constantly being sexually assaulted and raped by different soldiers including this accused. These two girls, however, were not the only victims who suffered at the hands of Dragan Zelenovic. He admitted his participation in the rape and gang-rape of other unidentified women and thereby victimised numerous women and girls. All victims were terrorised and endured inordinate physical and mental suffering. Not only did they is suffer the pain, indignity, and humiliation of being repeatedly violated, but they also did not know whether there it would survive this ordeal. The victims were unarmed, defenceless female civilians. They were made even more vulnerable by being detained under inhumane conditions and transferred from detention centre to detention centre. They experienced starvation, lack of sleep, and filthy living conditions during these times. As a result of the repeated sexual assaults under these conditions, the physical and psychological health of many of the victims seriously deteriorated or was destroyed. None of these victims will ever be able to forget. Not all of them will be able to heal. Some may continue to be haunted and tormented for the rest of their lives by what they were put through by this accused and his co-perpetrators. Let us now turn to the aggravating and mitigating factors. The Prosecution submits that pursuant to paragraph 15 of the plea agreement the following aggravating factors must be taken into account when determining the sentence for Mr. Zelenovic: First, the particular vulnerability of victim FWS-75 due to her youthful age of only 15 years at the time. Second, the multiplicity of the rapes. The Prosecution submits that there are also mitigating factors that should be taken into account in this specific case. The most important mitigating circumstance is the fact that the accused entered into a guilty plea and accepted his responsibility for the crimes described. He has cooperated with the Prosecution in achieving the plea agreement and has provided truthful and complete information. As the Prosecution submitted in its sentencing brief, the plea of guilty should be regarded as a mitigating factor for two reasons. First, if it is entered before the start of the trial, it does save the victims and witnesses from testifying and having to give evidence. It also may substantial of time and resources. Most importantly, however, and in particular in cases involving heinous crimes like rape and torture and where victims and witnesses have already testified once, like in the instance case in the Kunarac trial, it does avoid additional hardship for the victims, witnesses, and their families, and it does avoid the danger of potential retraumatisation. In this regard the Prosecution notes the Defence expert report provided by Ana Najman, specialist in medical clinical psychology titled, "Attitude Toward Trauma and the Act of Rape by Victims and Perpetrator," which deals extensively with the characteristics of rape committed in armed conflict, the trauma suffered by rape victims, and the positive impact of the admission of guilt by the perpetrator. The report was admitted as an annex to the Defence sentencing brief and the Prosecution concurs with and endorses this report and the findings made therein. Secondly, a guilty plea also contributes to the fulfillment of the objective of the Tribunal which is the establishment of the truth. In this particular case, the events that occurred in Foca and its surrounding villages in the first half of 1992 have already been established beyond reasonable doubt by two judgements of this Tribunal, both of which were upheld by the Appeals Chamber. These are the judgements in the cases Prosecutor versus Kunarac, Kovac, and Vukovic, and Prosecutor versus Krnojelac. Nevertheless, the guilty plea of Mr. Zelenovic contributes substantially to the Tribunal's mandate. This is because for the first time in the history of this Tribunal a perpetrator who has participated in these events actually admits and confirms what happened to the female non-Serb population in this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. Mr. Zelenovic's admission of guilt thereby contributes not only to establishing the truth but can be hoped to also contribute to the reconciliation process in the area. The Prosecution thus concurs with the Defence that the admission of guilt by the accused should mitigate his sentence. The Defence in it's sentencing brief submitted on 14 February 2007 further argued that a number of personal circumstances should be taken into account as mitigating factors. It is noted that Article 24, paragraph (2) of the Statute requires the Trial Chamber to take into account "the individual circumstances of the convicted person" in the course of determining sentence. The Appeals Chamber in Prosecutor versus Kunarac held that family concerns should in principle be a mitigating factor. In the instant case the accused has submitted that he is married and has a minor son and that he is a war invalid with 80 per cent established disability. The Prosecution concurs with the Defence that the Trial Chamber take into account the family situation of the accused as a mitigating factor. However, in view of the number and severity of crimes committed by the accused, it is submitted that this factor can only have limited mitigating impact on the sentence to be meted out. The same applies in the Prosecution's submissions with regard to the other mitigating factors set forth by the Defence in its sentencing brief. These are the facts that the accused has no previous conviction, that he comported well while in the UN detention facility and that he has certain health issues. The Prosecution agrees that such circumstances generally can mitigate an accused's penalties to a limited extent. It must not be overlooked, however, that such factors can only relate to the assessment of a penalty. They cannot derogate the gravity of the crime. Again, in view of the number and severity of the crimes committed by the accused, it is submitted that these factors can only have very limited mitigating impact. The last factor to be considered in the sentencing by the Trial Chamber is the sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia. Pursuant to Article 24 and Rule 101, the Trial Chamber is required to take into account these practices. As the Prosecution submitted in its brief, Article 142 of the SFRY Criminal Code encompasses criminal offences against humanitarian and international law, penalising inter alia crimes against humanity. The sentencing range for perpetrators of such crimes lies between the minimum sentence of no less than 5 years and the maximum penalty of death. It has been established by the Appeals Chamber in Tadic and Kunarac that a Trial Chamber must consider but is not bound by the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia. I will now come to the conclusions. In conclusion of these arguments, the Prosecution respectfully requests that the Trial Chamber impose a sentence upon Mr. Zelenovic commensurate to the gravity of the offences he committed. When doing so, the Trial Chamber should take into account that the accused has admitted his guilt and accepted his responsibility. Balancing the severe gravity of the crimes committed and the mitigating effect of the accused's acceptance of guilt and responsibility, it is submitted that the term of imprisonment within the range of 10 to 15 years would be the appropriate sentence. In submitting this term of imprisonment, the Prosecution took into account the sentences meted out against the co-perpetrators Kunarac, Kovac, and Vukovic for similar crimes committed in the same context. Their sentences amount to 28, 20, and 12 years respectively. Notably the, 12-year sentence was given to the accused Vukovic for the commission of a single rape as a crime against humanity. The Prosecution is aware that the sentence requested for Mr. Zelenovic is comparatively low, but contrary to these convicted persons, Mr. Zelenovic has decided to face his guilt and to publicly accept full responsibility for the heinous acts he committed. He expressed regret and remorse for his victims. In this regard, the Prosecution draws the attention of the Trial Chamber to the signed statement of the accused dated 9 February, which was annexed to the Defence sentencing brief in which Mr. Zelenovic expressed his remorse for the victims and his hope that his admissions -- admissions will contribute to reconciliation. It is submitted that for these reasons and notwithstanding the severe character of the crimes he committed it is justified that his sentence is considerably lower than the sentences given to the accused in the Kunarac et al. case. This completes my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. Jovanovic, I think it would be fair to grant you also 37 minutes instead of 25. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As my learned friend has already spoken about the procedural history of this case, I will not go into it, and this will save time. My learned friend has also given an overview of the factual basis, and the Defence did not deal with this in its brief apart from saying that this has already been established and that Mr. Zelenovic has accepted it. Therefore, the Defence will not deal with this aspect either in our oral submissions. What I wish to draw attention to in particular are the mitigating circumstances mentioned in the brief of the 14th of February, 2007. All the arguments that have already been put forward show that Mr. Zelenovic sincerely accepts his guilt, that he absolutely accepts his responsibility, that he is willing to be punished in any way that this Chamber deems appropriate, and the Defence wishes to point out the significance of his admission of guilt, especially with reference to the gravity of the crimes that have been established. The Defence fully agrees with the Prosecution position and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal as regards the crime of rape. This is a heinous crime, and the Defence and Mr. Zelenovic himself do not wish in any way to diminish the significance of this crime and its gravity. However, the effort made by Mr. Zelenovic in admitting to these crimes and his expressed desire to protect the victims, to apologise to them, and by his admission justify the work and existence of this Tribunal are, in my view, a mitigating circumstance which must be taken into account and given due weight. The International Criminal Tribunal, as has been pointed out more than once, is now implementing its completion strategy. Madam Carla Del Ponte, the Chief Prosecutor, is constantly undertaking diplomatic missions, a we hear that she is constantly assuring various governments and international institutions that this Tribunal will fulfil its mission. Unfortunately, we see that there are still accused at large and, unfortunately, we also hear that there are those who challenge and deny the results of this Tribunal. Mr. Zelenovic's admission of guilt clearly indicates that there were crimes, that these crimes did happen, and this has also been repeated in his statement of remorse. All this shows that this Court really needed to be established and that it is in fact fulfilling its purpose. Mr. Zelenovic has admitted his guilt. He did so within a very short time of his arrival in the Detention Unit of the ICTY. It was done as quickly as technically feasible in view of the talks between the Prosecution and the Defence. It was done much sooner than a trial date could be set, for example, or an 11 bis motion lodged. By doing this, Mr. Zelenovic has saved the Tribunal considerable time and resources. Mr. Zelenovic, as can be seen in the brief and the expert report appended to it, spared the victims retraumatisation which would have resulted from their having to testify. I only wish to draw attention to the fact that these persons testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Kunarac et al., but that now they are needed as witnesses before the national courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So they are continuing to undergo these difficult experiences having to face the Court, having to face Defence counsel, and answer questions in proceedings. Mr. Zelenovic has spared them this additional effort. The expert report explains the lengthy nature of the healing of these persons and how they can be exposed to fresh suffering through having to mention all the details of the events which occurred. Dragan Zelenovic was a member of the army of Republika Srpska. He was a private, an ordinary soldier, a military policeman, and, as stated by the Prosecution, he was one of those who participated in these events before the rapes and torture took place, who participated in the armed conflict that occurred on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He certainly did participate in this, but he was only a small part of this, at the lowest level of responsibility. Unfortunately, in the description of the crimes accepted by Mr. Zelenovic, we see that these events also occurred with the participation of unidentified soldiers. These are people who are perhaps still at large today. However, Mr. Zelenovic through his admission of guilt has decided to face his own responsibility and accepted that these events occurred. His admission of guilt shows beyond any doubt what actually happened on the territory of Foca and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The personal circumstances of Mr. Zelenovic have also been put forward. He is in very poor health, which can be seen in the report submitted by the doctor of the Detention Unit. Mr. Zelenovic is an invalid, and his disability amounts to 80 per cent. He has sincerely expressed his remorse, and he will repeat the statement already appended to the brief of the of the 14th of February, 2007. The Prosecution and the Defence have put forward their proposals as to sentencing, 7 to 10 years, or 10 to 15 years respectively, and the only point of agreement is a 10-year sentence. The Defence is fully aware of the gravity of the crimes committed. It is also aware of fact that in view of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal one cannot simply compare sentences between cases because each case is unique and has specific circumstances involved. Also, the fact that Mr. Zelenovic was only a common private doesn't necessarily have to have special weight in sentencing, if we look at those who were accused and sentenced before this Tribunal and who held high rank, either in military or political structures. I will, however, draw attention to something that has been stated in the Defence brief, and that is the standpoint of the Trial Chamber in the Todorovic case where Todorovic's crimes were found to be extremely heinous and his behaviour very cruel, but he was sentenced to 10 years, with the explanation that the sentence would have to be much longer if the facts had had to be established in trial proceedings. I will also mention the case of Prosecutor versus Biljana Plavsic, where someone who was in the highest echelons of power and whose influence extended throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in the armed conflict was sentenced to 11 years. Mr. Zelenovic fully agreed to cooperate with the Prosecution. He undertook to cooperate in every way required by the Office of the Prosecutor. He undertook to make any statement to the Office of the Prosecutor and to testify in any case, in any proceedings in this Tribunal. A short time has elapsed from Mr. Zelenovic's guilty plea, and for this reason he has not had an opportunity to demonstrate his cooperation in practice, but we must take his cooperation to be full, because he has expressed his standpoint in this respect. These are in brief the arguments put forward in the Defence brief. The Defence abides by its arguments and its proposal as to sentencing. Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Zelenovic, by Your Honours' leave, will make his statement of remorse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, counsel requested to give you an opportunity to give a statement. He already announced what kind of statement it would be. You have an opportunity to address the Court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have expressed my position and remorse in the statement presented by the Defence. Also now, before all, I wish to repeat this and say I thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you first and foremost with a few words and then all those who advocate truth and justice. I hope that the victims of this senseless war will hear my words too. This is a war that didn't make anybody happy. Guided by Biblical teachings that the truth is not to be feared because that is the only thing that will help all, I have confessed as to my guilt, and I am prepared to bear all the consequences of that. I know that not a single form of punishment can erase the suffering sustained by my victims. However, faith teaches us that admission of having committed injustice to someone is the best way of helping them. And also in order to protect the victims from being reminded yet again of their suffering, I admitted my guilt. I feel sorry for all the victims who were victimised by anything that I did, and that is why I express from this forum my deepest remorse and regret. I am a human being with virtues and vices, and I didn't know how to deal with these vices when I should have. Your Honours, it is for you to give your say now. I will courageously take any sentence meted out, and I hope that God will give me strength to go through all of this and that I go back to my family. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the Judges may have some questions to the parties. Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. Maybe I would like to address myself to Mr. Zelenovic, now that he has also said a few words. I just want to ask -- you may be seated, Mr. Zelenovic. You may be seated. I just want to find out from you, Mr. Zelenovic, when you began to feel the remorse.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the indictment was issued against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I started believing in God. Until then I had not believed in God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was when was this? When was the indictment issued against you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995, 1996. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you come into the custody of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I came from Russia. I came to the prison here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you go to Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the year 2000 -- 2001, that is, on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why did you go to Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I went. I went to work there, and there was this indictment issued against me, as you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The indictment was issued against you by your own admission in 1995, 1996. In 2000, 2001, you go to Russia and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- at the time in 1995 and 1996 when the indictment was issued against you, you were already remorseful. You are now a believer, and you decided to go to Russia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You decided not to come and hand yourself over and say you want to face the consequences like you say you want to face them today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. But that is what the policy was before that. Everybody was saying that it's a political court here. I'm not a politician. I just listened to what others said, and I just went to Russia. They simply removed me. They said, "Go to Russia. Go to Russia." I was just a mere rubber stamp. I mean, I was but a pawn in all these games.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, I'm talking to you about Mr. Zelenovic, not about other people. Yes, sir. Do you want to say something, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. By your leave I'd like to give a clarification, an explanation in terms of the time and way in which Mr. Zelenovic went to Russia. I can deal with that after you have concluded your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will deal with that after I have concluded my questions. Let me deal with Mr. Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, you have just told us this morning that you became a believer when you received the indictment in 1995, 1996. Now, when those who told you to go to Russia told you to do that, why didn't you say to them, "I'm sorry. I want to face the music. I am a believer. I was wrong. I know I did wrong. I know I've hurt them, and I want to go and face my victims and apologise to them. I am not going to Russia"? Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was thinking about what would happen to my family afterwards. That's why I did what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what did you think would happen to your family afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how can I know? Quite simply when they say go, go somewhere else, end of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who says go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People, people from the association. Do you understand that? I mean, the people in Russia that I socialised with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand. The people in Russia tell you to leave Bosnia, to go to Russia. Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who are the people who said to you, "Go to Russia"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Russian people that I socialised with in Belgrade. I first went to Belgrade, to Serbia. And it was from Serbia that I went to Russia, yes. And I have a Serbian passport there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you went to Russia under a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because you didn't want to be detected, Mr. Zelenovic, is that a fact? You know, you have confessed to your guilt. I can't understand --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- why you are now trying to beat about the bush. You were trying to conceal your identity. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not hiding the fact that I went to Russia. And I started thinking about what it was that I did when I went to prison. I had plenty of time to lie down, look at the ceiling, and wonder why it was that I was in prison. I was in Russia in prison for 11 months, and that is when I realised everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, please listen to my questions and answer my questions, okay? If you have to tell a story, you can ask for an opportunity to do so. My question to you is: You went to Russia under a false name; is that correct? Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you did so because you wanted to evade detection for these crimes isn't that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you were a fugitive from justice there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact it is not correct today to say you felt the remorse in 1995, 1996. You are not telling the truth when you say so, isn't it so, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you how it was. I started thinking about what it was that I did when the indictment was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, listen to my question and answer my question. You did not feel remorse in 1995, 1996, say? Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. That's when the indictment was issued against me, and that's when I started thinking, and that's when I started repenting. Yes. Yes. Until the indictment was issued against me, I didn't even think about this. As time went by, I kept thinking about it more and more until I came to prison in Russia. Then I truly realised that -- then I really started thinking about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic, you -- you felt remorse on the 9th of February, 2007, when you signed the statement because you had no escape. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no. No, no. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- were you with your family in Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where was your family when you were in Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How old is your minor son, sir, today, as we speak?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what does your wife do?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She works in a company. She's a secretary in this organisation where I had worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact, Mr. Zelenovic, you abandoned not only the victims of your crimes but also your family to go to Russia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I haven't seen my son in five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, sir. Out of choice, in fact, because you decided to abandon your son and go to Russia. So it doesn't really matter how long you go to gaol.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't matter how long you don't see him for?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what do you mean it doesn't matter? That is the thing that contributed the most of all for me to come to this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. But you were arrested in Russia. You didn't come on your own, sir. Let's look at the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't come voluntarily. It didn't matter how long you stayed away from your family. If you were not arrested, you'd still be in Russia even now. So it really doesn't matter how long you stay away from them, from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not so, no. Again, I'm telling you. I'm telling you how it was. How can I now say that I didn't want to see my own child?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're telling me, but the facts speak contrary to what you are telling us. Thank you very much, Mr. Zelenovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions as well. I will not further explore, Mr. Zelenovic, the issue raised by Judge Moloto, that is how you balanced over a longer period of time the interests of others and your own interests not to be arrested. I have -- Mr. Jovanovic, I have first of all a very practical question. In the detention order, the -- well, let me say the Russian detention order, at the bottom there is some language which says: "I received the order on the 23rd of April, 2005." First of all, I had some difficulties to find this in the original, and of course the date of the 23rd of April, 2005, was quite a puzzle to me. Perhaps it's somewhere at the back of that document. We have received a photocopy, which is not -- especially at the end not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the date of this decision made by the Office of the Prosecution of the Russian Federation is the 23rd of August, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the last line above the -- I would say the second signature, is that the line that reads: "I received the order on the 23rd of --" I have difficulties in identifying 23rd, but that's the 23rd of August. So there is a translation error where it says "April." Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Obviously it's an error. In the original decision that I have here, the date is the 23rd of August, 2005, as well as the date when the decision was received by Mr. Zelenovic, and he signed for that, but under the name of Branislav Petrovic. That is precisely the question that I wanted to clarify when I spoke during the questions put by His Honour Judge Moloto. Mr. Zelenovic was indeed in Russia, and he knew that he had been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. The indictment was actually from 1999, but as he said, he started thinking about all of these events in 1995. In actual fact, Mr. Zelenovic was told to leave Foca. As he said, he came to the Republic of Serbia. Regrettably the Defence did not have the personal documents of Mr. Zelenovic in order to submit them along with this brief, that is to say those documents that were issued to him in the name of Branislav Petrovic in 2001 in Serbia. Actually, in 2001, Mr. Zelenovic went to the police station in Belgrade where documents were issued to him, a passport with a visa of the Russian Federation, and a personal identity card in the name of Branislav Petrovic. I'm convinced that it was known what his identity was and through these documents a suggestion was directly made to him that he was supposed to leave. Mr. Zelenovic knew that he was indicted, as I've already said. That does not diminish his responsibility. His choice could have been to surrender to the International Criminal Tribunal. However, if he receives documents that are not falsified, that were not bought on the black market, but that were issued by the official authorities of the Republic of Serbia, he quite simply acted in accordance with that. But as I've said, that does not diminish the fact in any way that he knew that he had been indicted and that he could have found a way of surrendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let me try to understand this. Let me try to understand. You say these documents was not falsified. It was clear to Mr. Zelenovic that the name on this document was not his but the photograph was his. How possibly could you explain to us that these were regular documents, because that's what I understand you to tell us. I do understand that they were not stolen, that there was no forgery sought by Mr. Zelenovic, but how could he possibly understand these documents which changed his identity to be regularly issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely. I said that they were just formally issued in a regular procedures -- in a regular procedure. These documents obviously conceal Mr. Zelenovic's identity. But if we can say that the official authorities of a state issue a forgery, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand the situation that although Mr. Zelenovic, who says, "I started thinking about what happened and I felt remorse," that nevertheless in his conduct he was more guided by official authorities, more people who would fell him to leave Foca, to leave Belgrade, he was more guided by those signals, by those -- and not that much, at least at that time by his remorse towards the victims. Is that a correct understanding of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Unfortunately that's the way it is. I said something about that in my own remarks when I spoke. The situation in the states the former Yugoslavia is such that there is a negative attitude towards this Tribunal and regrettably that is how Mr. Zelenovic acted. This was not purely an autonomous decision. It was not his decision only not to respond or not to face up to his responsibility already at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. I think, Mr. Zelenovic, you would like to add something. I'll give you an opportunity soon to do so. Before we further -- still looking at the -- at the Russian document, I think that the parties do not fully agree whether the detention started on the 22nd or the 23rd of August, 2005, or at least what should be taken into consideration. Ms. Moeller, do you take 22nd of August as the starting date of detention, or would you consider the 23rd to be the first day of detention, because it was then only that a detention order was issued after Mr. Zelenovic was arrested the day before?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would -- we would argue the 23rd was the first day of detention for the accused and it should start from then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 23rd. That is not the arrest but the detention order. Mr. Jovanovic, what be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Zelenovic was arrested on the 22nd of August by the police of the Russian Federation but there was a detention order issued on the 23rd of August, 2005, based on the request of this Tribunal and that is the day when his detention began under the name of Branislav Petrovic, at the demand of the ICTY and after his identity was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not understand the language of -- let me just look at the Rule. "Detained in custody pending surrender." You exclude from that deprivation of liberty as a factual consequence of arrest, and you take it that it starts with a detention order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the decision of the Prosecution of the Russian Federation establishing that Mr. Zelenovic is to be detained at the request of the ICTY bears the date the 23rd of August, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Mr. Jovanovic, you suggested that Mr. Zelenovic was very quick in admitting guilt, even before, as you said, the 11 bis hearing could be scheduled, I think you said, or let me just -- well, you said something in relation to that. You also suggested that by admitting guilt that the resources of this Tribunal would be under a less burden compared to the situation where a 11 bis proceedings would have been followed. Could you tell us why you think sentencing proceedings take less time than 11 bis proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The fact is that the 11 bis hearing was held before Mr. Zelenovic admitted his guilt, but no decision was issued. Mr. Zelenovic was indicted by the ICTY, detained by the ICTY, and I believe it must be taken that he is under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. As there is no 11 bis decision, we have to assume he would have been tried before this Tribunal. That's why I pointed out that his admission of guilt several months after he arrived in the Detention Unit of this Tribunal represents a saving of time and resources for this Tribunal. We cannot assert that this case would have been transferred to the national courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina because we have no decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you said, Mr. Jovanovic, was that it was done as quickly as technically feasible in view of the talks between the Prosecution and the Defence. It was done much sooner than a trial date could be set, for example, or an 11 bis motion lodged. You are, at that time, not talking about whether or not there was a decision, but you emphasised how quick it was, whereas looking at the history, I see that we start with a -- I think a delayed plea. Then we get a plea of not guilty, then an 11 bis motion was filed, and from what I remember, even heard or about to be heard. Just -- it would take us drafting one decision and that would have been all the burden for this Tribunal, apart from what it would take -- of course, the decision could be either that Mr. Zelenovic would be tried before this Tribunal or be sent back, and there was a fair chance that 11 bis would -- would take far less time for this Tribunal than -- of course, depending on the outcome. But nevertheless, you are suggesting that by at that point in time to enter a guilty plea that even in relation to 11 bis proceedings it would have saved quite some time for this Tribunal, which is, I wouldn't say impossible, but is not the logical consequence of that decision taken at that stage in the pending proceedings. Would you agree with me, or would you respond to that in a different way? Is my understanding wrong or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will give you the history. When Mr. Zelenovic arrived in the Detention Unit of the ICTY there was certain problems with the appointment of counsel, and that was the reason his first plea hearing was postponed. After I was appointed Mr. Zelenovic's counsel the 11 bis motion was lodged. There was disclosure on several occasions, and as Defence counsel, I had to be familiar with the materials. After going through the materials disclosed to me and during the disclosure itself, the Defence contacted the Prosecution. A factual basis was agreed and finally a plea agreement was reached. If we take it that the 11 bis decision would have been to refer this case to the national court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then of course we could not speak of any saving of time for this Tribunal. However, it is a fact that Mr. Zelenovic is here and we cannot pre-judge the outcome of the 11 bis proceedings. The Defence opposed the request by the OTP under Rule 11 bis. We can only assume what the decision would have been, but the state of facts right now is that there is no indictment against Mr. Zelenovic before the national court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he is now in detention set by this Tribunal, and that it is before this Tribunal that he has pleaded guilty. So he is now under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. So what you're actually saying is that the effect on 11 bis proceedings is rather speculative because we would not know what the outcome would have been. That would have been both, positive speculation and negative speculation. Yes? I see you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by the medical report which speaks about smoking history and about smoking. Is smoking history for Mr. Zelenovic or is it still -- still a habit? Nothing -- I'm not expressing any positive or negative judgement on that, but I just would like to know whether he gave up smoking or whether he still smokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the health report was compiled by the doctor of the Detention Unit based on specialist examinations, some in hospital. Mr. Zelenovic spent some time in hospital outside the Detention Unit. His health --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I have read the report. I fully understand it. The only thing I'd like to know, whether the present situation is one Mr. Zelenovic is suffering consequences of his smoking he had in the past which he gave up, or whether he still smokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Zelenovic no longer smokes, and he has been described by the Detention Unit doctor as a very disciplined patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zelenovic, when did you give up smoking? Could you tell it us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a smoker for 30 years. I never stopped. When an X-ray was taken of my lungs here, Dr. Falke told me, "Half of your lungs are no longer working, and if you don't stop smoking, you're finished." Then I was asked by Mr. McFadden for an interview, and he offered me some pills to help me stop smoking. And when I started taking these pills I stopped smoking and now I no longer smoke. Two days ago, I went to the hospital again, and all the check-ups were done all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when was that that Mr. McFadden offered you the pills?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As soon as I arrived and the first X-ray was done. When I arrived from Russia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least congratulations with that step in your life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me see whether I have any other questions. No. At this moment I have no further questions. I suggest this, Mr. Zelenovic, you said you wished to say something else. Then we will have the break. During the break the Judges will discuss whether they have any further questions. If so, they will put them to the parties, to you, Mr. Zelenovic. Then the parties will have an opportunity to make some closing remarks, and then we'll adjourn after having given Mr. Zelenovic an opportunity to speak last. I do know that this is not within the -- I would say the adversarial tradition, but nevertheless it's not forbidden either. So Mr. Zelenovic will be given an opportunity to say something at the end and then we will adjourn and consider whether and when to give a decision. Mr. Zelenovic, you have an opportunity because you -- you gave me a signal that you'd like to add something to -- I would say mainly to the Russian story, I think it was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes. Because when I arrived in Russia, I spent four or five years there and nothing happened. All of a sudden when Milosevic fell ill they arrested me on the 21st. I was in Siberia. It's a place that's four hours by plane from Moscow. I lived there with a woman who is also a lawyer. They said to me, "Dragan, you're under arrest. There is an Interpol warrant out for your arrest. We are not cooperating with them. We'll release you." They said to me, "We do not cooperate with The Hague Tribunal." That was the 20 -- that was why there's a confusion about the 21st or the 23rd of August. They arrested me and released me and said, "You're free." But then on the 23rd they arrested me again and they said, "We have to wait for a report from Moscow to see what Moscow says." When they put me in prison, the prison was awful. I fell ill when I got to that prison. I asked to be taken to The Hague, but they said, "We're going to give you a false passport." And I said, "Give me the original passport." And they said no. And in the April they took me to the airports in Moscow. When I arrived at the airport in Moscow they said, "Milosevic is dead. There's nothing doing, you're going to another prison." And then I said, "Do you want me to wait for somebody else to fall ill and then you'll send me to The Hague again." And they said, "No, no, you're going to another prison." And then when Milosevic died, and that's why they said I was arrested on the 24th of April, and they sent me to another prison, Nizevatovsi [phoen], and there I spent 21 days and then they sent me back to the court in Hanti-Mansiysk [phoen], and there the court released me. It acquitted me, and they told me I was free, and then they took me to the prison to take my things, and they said, "You're under arrest again." And I said, "Why?" And they said, "We don't know what Moscow will say." And they kept me there in detention for a month. And then when the question was to whether to release me or send me to Yugoslavia or send me to The Hague they said, "We don't cooperate with The Hague Tribunal. You're going to Sarajevo." And then they transferred me to Sarajevo. And when I arrived in Sarajevo, my counsel at the time, Dusko Orasanin, I said to him, "If I go to The Hague, I will speak the truth." That's as concerns my passport. They knew I was in Russia all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps -- thank you, Mr. Zelenovic, please be seated. Perhaps it would be good if the parties would consider whether they are in a position to provide any documentation about the detention since the 23rd of August, because this Chamber, of course, will have to consider what time to be deduced under Rule 01 -- is it 101? Let me just have a look. Yes. "Detained in custody pending surrender to the Tribunal or pending trial or appeal." The story is a bit confusing at the moment. There was an arrest, then there was an immediate release, from what I understand, then there was a detention order on the 23rd of August, then later on it became -- well, Mr. Zelenovic will have an opportunity to add something, that on from that time it was at moments - that's at least how I understand it - unclear whether this detention continued for the purposes of this Tribunal. Mr. Zelenovic explained something to us. I would say it adds rather to my confusion than anything else, but perhaps the parties, there must be a kind of detention history, and perhaps the parties could consider whether there is any possibility to get these things clear. I think it's -- both parties could even work together on it because of course we want to fairly apply Rule 101(C) also to Mr. Zelenovic. Mr. Zelenovic, you again indicated that -- there's something with a -- yes. Yes, Mr. Zelenovic. If I misunderstood you, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenovic -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never released. The court acquitted me. And when I came to the prison to take my bag they shut me up again. So I was in prison all the time. I have those documents. The Court acquitted me. But when I got to the prison, they locked me up again and they said, "We'll wait to see what Moscow says." And then I sat there for another month without any indictment. And then from that prison I flew to Moscow and then to Sarajevo. I have all those documents, and my counsel has all the documents as to when I was detained in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have of course we have seen the detention it order, Mr. Jovanovic. We have also seen the decision of the BiH court. If there is anything more or if there is agreement on what actually happened as far as detention is concerned, the Chamber would be assisted by receiving that information. Not necessarily at this very moment. What we'll do now is we'll have a break for half an hour. I suggest to the parties that apart from whether we have any additional questions to the parties or to Mr. Zelenovic that for final submissions 15 minutes. Would that be a reasonable suggestion, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, 15 minutes, would that do as well for a final submission, oral submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, yes. The Defence has actually already presented its arguments, so I will be very brief. Basically I've said what there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm not forcing you to use the full 15 minutes. We'll adjourn and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to put -- well, first give an opportunity to Judge Van Den Wyngaert to put an additional question, and I would have one and a half questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I have one additional question, Mr. Zelenovic, and the question is the following: You pled guilty, and my question is to what extent your desire not to be sent back under Article 11 bis is an element in your guilty plea. Is that something that is part of your motivation or doesn't it have anything to do with it? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm telling you I wanted to tell the truth and I confessed as to what had happened, and I am prepared to bear full responsibility for that. I admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Is it also an element in your decision that you prefer to be -- the rest of your trial to be held here rather than in Bosnia? Is that an element in your guilty plea or doesn't it have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no, no. Nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a question to the parties. The last remaining count is -- I'll briefly call it the rape count close to the fish restaurant where only rape is charged and not torture. This concerns two known and two unidentified victims. It's not entirely clear from the context, although there are indicia for it, that the unidentified women were also of Muslim ethnicity. Do the parties agree on that? Is that part of the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As far as the Prosecution is concerned, I think they were also of non-Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that also the position the Defence takes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, generally the events described in the indictment and the crimes committed by Mr. Zelenovic were committed on a discriminatory basis. However, if what is stated is that these are persons unidentified, then that directly shows that the identity is known in a way, but the Defence agrees that the crimes were committed on a discriminatory basis and that the victims in the crimes described were women of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Having clarified this, now my following question to you, Ms. Moeller, would be there was -- there were a few questions and a few answers in relation to this incident during the -- during the hearing in January. The Chamber was asking questions to Madam Uertz-Retzlaff in relation to how this incident was charged, as rape only, not as torture. We then got an answer saying that since it was not in any context of interrogation or investigation that the Prosecution focused here on rape and not on torture, and I just will read a few lines from the transcript. I said: "So, do I understand you well that you say that by the incident near to the fish restaurant there was not, like in other situations, intimidation of third persons?" Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, "Yes." And I continued, "Third persons who were observing the victims for purposes of taking away where to that extent there were not third persons present there." And Madam Uertz-Retzlaff said, "Yes, Your Honour. That was the distinction I think that we made at." And then I said, "Well, there's still discrimination, or is it not?" Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, "Yes, Your Honour." And I said, "So for that reason torture could have been there under --", and Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, "Yes, but we've chosen not to do that. We have chosen not to charge in relation to this incident." Now, my question to you is the following: A discriminatory intent could be an aggravating circumstance in relation to rape. Discriminatory intent is not an element of the crime of rape. Now, we see the following situation: Both parties agree that the women raped there were not of Serbian ethnicity. I just heard Mr. Jovanovic saying that Defence accepts that the -- all the rapes why committed with a discriminatory intent. The parties seem to agree on that. Now, the Prosecution has deliberately chosen not to charge torture, also not, as explained by Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, although there was a discriminatory element, a factual discriminatory element threw but you have chosen not to charge torture but only rape. Do you think that the Prosecution, and even the question not only whether you could, but whether you argue that nevertheless do you argue that the discriminatory intent could be taken as a circumstance where you deliberately refrained from charging which one would expect this rape as torture because of that discriminatory element? Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address this issue. We will submit that first of all that it's not the discrimination intent which makes the acts the crime as a crime of torture. It's -- it's -- we would submit that it's the purpose of the intimidation, it's the purpose of violent acts, it's the purpose of the rape which may make these acts the crime of torture. In particular, for instance, if force is used to get information from the victims as we have in some instances in this case, these acts would be -- would be qualified as torture. But the rape itself is -- is a crime which does not need to have elements of torture and -- first of all. Secondly, the discriminatory ground can be -- may be taken into account in seen it issued for crime of torture regardless whether the accused is -- also committed any other crimes, including torture. So what I'm saying that the crime of rape may be committed on discriminatory grounds without having any elements of torture and without having the accused charged with torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me then try to take you back to the language of how I understand torture to be, that is that rape would also be torture if it would be committed with the aim at obtaining information or a confession. You just alluded to that already. Or at punishing, intimidating or coercing the person or a third person or at discriminating on any ground against the victim or a third person. Now, apart from that, it's clear that certainly as explained there were no third persons involved. There was no investigation. There was no interrogation at the time. Nevertheless, if committed as one of the options for the purpose of, or at least with the intent to discriminate on any grounds against the victim or third person, would have justified charging torture next to rape, rape understood as not necessarily with discriminatory or any of the other grounds torture. Now, you refrain from qualifying this rape as torture as well. Do you still think that the discriminative elements could be considered an aggravating circumstance to, I would say, a rape without any further qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Again, as we see the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and as the Judge has already mentioned, that unless the discrimination is element of the crime like in persecution, it can be considered as an aggravating factor for the crimes, for other crimes listed under Article 5, including rape, including torture, and in this case we can see that those who were selected for rape were selected on discriminatory ground and they were subjected to crime of rape. They were raped by the accused, and so discriminatory ground is present but not as element of the crime and not as -- and not as inherent part of this crime of rape. So it can be considered as an aggravating factor and we would submit it should be considered as an aggravating factor on this case again on the basis of this two main considerations. First of all it's not element of the rape, and secondly it is not the inherent part of the -- of this crime of rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're not addressing the -- but perhaps I've not been clear enough. You're not addressing what is my real problem. My problem is not whether a rape with discriminatory intent could be charged and then discriminatory intent to be taken into account as an aggravating element. My question is more of a procedural nature where on all rapes you charge in addition torture and then asked about why it was not done in this fish restaurant, rape, the answer was there were no third persons involved. Our question there was: But still there was the discriminatory element. And then the answer is: We have decided not to charge that as torture. Whether by that decision you did not deprive yourself from the right to invoke discriminatory -- the discriminatory element as an aggravating circumstance because you took distance from that by not charging it like you had done on all the others. So it's more a procedural question rather than understanding the substantive case law of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. Apparently the Prosecution just exercised its discretionary power not to charge with this crime, the accused, but as to the -- taking into account the discriminatory nature of his acts still the Prosecution think that this factor should be taken into account in sentencing, which means that despite the fact that in this specific incident the Prosecution decided not to go ahead with the torture charges, the Prosecution position is that as to the rape, which is still in this count, with regard to rape the discriminatory -- discriminatory intention be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it now has procedural consequences that -- even under these very specific circumstances where all the other rapes were accompanied by torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just the Prosecution exercise its discretionary power. We think that it doesn't affect the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's a clear position. I'd like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make final submissions, not necessarily taking 15 minutes. And of course, Mr. Jovanovic, if you make your final submissions, of course you could still address the matter just raised because the Chamber would like to hear the position of the Defence on that as well. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very short and try to save some of the plus time that I used up this morning in the opening where I miscalculated a little bit. First I would like to address one issue that came up when Your Honour Judge Moloto put some questions to the accused, namely the question of when the first indictment was issued.
