I checked that and the first indictment on which Mr. Zelenovic's name occurs was signed by His Honour Judge Richard Goldstone on 19 June 1996. Maybe that assists the Court. Then regarding Your Honour Judge Orie's question regarding documents relate together detention period of the accused in Russia. To my knowledge, the Prosecution office here does not have any detailed documentation of this period. However, we will try to request whether maybe the Court in Bosnia and Herzegovina has such documents and make them available if we should be able to obtain them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or even getting together with Mr. Jovanovic and to see what could be reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this respect is -- would certainly help.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that. Then there was some discussion about the plea agreement in relation to the aspect of time and resources that may be saved through the plea agreement and which mitigating effect this could have. We submit once more that this is certainly a very minor factor that should not dominate any sentencing considerations at all. The real value of this plea agreement as the Prosecution sees it, and the real impact it has is on the victim and the witnesses, and we do submit there it has some considerable weight, positive weight. We see it every day here in ongoing proceedings in the Tribunal that it is very difficult for witnesses to come back and testify a second time or even a third time. And this applies extremely to witnesses who were rape victims. It is very difficult for them to do it once, but to come here again and undergo the whole procedure again is very difficult, in particular, if it is some 15 years, like in this case, after the events happened and some five or six years after they first testified here. These witnesses try to move on with their lives. They try to heal as much as they can, and it is a big burden for them to -- to have to come back and testify again. And whether that be in a trial here or in a referral -- referral trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina does not make a difference, really, we think. So in this regard, we think the plea agreement must have a mitigating effect because it does contribute to the health and healing of the victims in this regard. Now, as to the other mitigating factors that were discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you say that the plea agreement that follows flight from justice has any weight and if it does to what extent on the saving of the resources of the Tribunal and all those involved in the tracking down and arrest of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I would say it does have weight. In the ideal world, of course, looking at this first indictment that I referred to, it contained eight accused, including the three accused which were already sentenced by the Court, Kunarac and his two co-accused, then some other persons who have deceased in the meantime and one perpetrator, Stankovic, who was referred down to the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, in the ideal world all of these eight perpetrators would of course have been tried here in one trial before this Tribunal. That would have been the proper course of justice. But unfortunately the de facto situation until today is that most trials have to start in the absence of co-accused because they don't surrender or they cannot be arrested and -- or for other reasons. It is very late, of course, for Mr. Zelenovic to plead guilty now, but we submit it is not too late. This Tribunal is still running. The victims are still it suffering from what they went through, and it still has an impact on whether or not a trial must be held once more about these events, and for this reason, because it does not now have to be held, we do submit it does save hardship for the witnesses and it does also save resources and time for the Tribunal as well as for local courts. Now, the other mitigating factors that have been addressed in this hearing as well, we already submitted in the beginning that in our submission they have to have very limited impact on -- on the sentencing considerations because of the extreme gravity of the crime. Now, some more facts have been adduced during this hearing, and I think it is up for Your Honours to consider taking into account these additional facts what weight, if any, to give to the personal circumstances of Mr. Zelenovic regarding his family situation, his health, et cetera. We will not comment further on that from the Prosecution's side. The last point I want to address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry to do this to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to cast any light on any medical attention that the accused might be receiving in detention, or is likely to receive if he goes to gaol?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, all detainees are under constant monitoring in the detention regarding their state of health, and many of the accused due to life circumstances or their age do have some medical issues indeed, and as far as we are aware they are probably being taken off -- taken care of by the Detention Unit, and should this accused be imprisonment and be transferred to one of states I think it has been assured bit registry who is in contact with these Member States of the UN who provide the prison for such detention that detainees also receive proper treatment there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The last question I would want to address shortly is remorse and the regret of the accused. We also heard some more from Mr. Zelenovic today about the circumstances as to when he first felt remorse and how it came about he decided to plead guilty to the crimes he committed, and it is obvious that his regret and remorse came late in the day and only came after an indictment had been issued against him. But still, I think it has to be given some weight because of the fact that he is one of the very few perpetrators here at this Tribunal who ever expressed any regret or remorse, and more importantly, who actually really took responsibility for what happened in the area and his individual acts. And in this context, even though there may be some question marks about the remorse and regret expressed, we do submit that it should be taken into account as a mitigating factor to some degree. In the overall assessment, as we submitted in the very beginning, the gravity of the crime is the single most important factor, and this together with the positive impact of the plea agreement we think are the most important considerations for Honourable Judges when deciding on the sentence of this accused. And I would complete my submissions on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question, Ms. Moeller. You said it has to be given some weight because of the fact that he is, is one of the very few perpetrators here at this Tribunal who have expressed any regret or remorse. Are you referring to the group of accused who have entered a guilty plea, or were you referring to the accused in general, because I have to dig deep in my memory to find a case of someone who pleaded guilty who did not express remorse, and I don't even know whether doing this digging exercise I would find any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand your point, and -- and I -- I think you're perfectly right. These perpetrators who decided to enter into a guilty plea usually also express their regress and remorse. So it seems these two things do go together, which is logical to some extent. What I was trying to say is, first of all, in this group of Foca-related perpetrators, whether it be the so-called female side of Foca, meaning all the things that happened to female inhabitants of Foca and its surrounding villages, or the male side, which was also subject to trials at this Tribunal, he is the only person who expressed remorse in front of this Tribunal. And I limit my remarks to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Jovanovic, it's your turn. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. By your leave, I wish to first refer to the issues raised today in the course of these proceedings. I submitted to the OTP the original document, the detention order of the Russian Federation. After detention was handed down on the 23rd of August, 2005, Mr. Zelenovic did not spend a single day out of detention. The detention was continuous until the moment he was transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. While in detention, pursuant to a warrant of the ICTY, he was fined by the court of the Russian Federation because he stayed in Russia beyond the deadline established in his visa. A visa issued by the Russian Federation implies that one must leave the country after a certain period of time, which he did not do and he was fined for this. However, the detention was continuous from the 23rd of August, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one specific question here? Did Mr. Zelenovic pay that fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was obliged to pay the fine, and I believe he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in many legal systems if you don't pay a fine it is substituted by detention. I'm just trying to find out whether any of this detention may have been for the reason of not paying the fine imposed due to -- to going -- to staying beyond the time that was determined in the visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. There was no decision handed down replacing the fine by a term in prison for reason of non-payment. There was only a fine, which he paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what the fine was, what was the amount?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I have, it was 20.000 rubles. Unfortunately I don't know what the exchange rate is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I. Perhaps Mr. Zelenovic could tell us what the exchange rate of a ruble is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 700 dollars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you paid it by your own means, Mr. Zelenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Jovanovic, that while in detention pursuant to an indictment by the ICTY he was detained by the Russian Federation. Do I understand you to say that he went beyond the visa permission while in detention or by the time he was detained had he already gone beyond the visa days, the visa period? In other words, I would like to understand whether -- was he being find for things that were impossible for him to comply with because he was in detention or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I understand it, after he was detained, when his documents were taken, it was established that he had not left Russia when he should have, and for this reason he was fined, when his documents were taken on detention. The detention itself was pursuant to the request of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would now like to briefly address some of the issues I raised previously and also some raised today. Mr. Zelenovic admitted his guilt thereby facing his own responsibility and confirming definitely that crimes of rape and torture as a form of crimes against humanity did happen during the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I feel that this is very important in view of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the processes now under way and that they represent a major contribution to reconciliation. Mr. Zelenovic underwent a process over time of thinking over what he had done. He has stated that he began this process in 1995 or 1996. The crimes were perpetrated in 1992. Mr. Zelenovic does not have a criminal record. He is not prone to commit crimes. He has faced his responsibility for what he did. He committed serious crimes. Had he thought about it, he would not have committed them. Over a period of time, thinking over what he had done, he came to the conclusion that he was responsible and expressed his remorse for his actions and regret for all the suffering of the victims. The fact that he did not face justice until the time of his arrest and all the circumstances attending this show that this was not his individual decision alone. Of course, his is the major share of responsibility for this, but I feel that the other circumstances which still exist have to be taken into consideration as there are a number of accused still at large, who you fugitives from justice and who could not be fugitives from justice if they were not receiving the support and assistance of others, including the state. Mr. Zelenovic, by his admission, made some restitution to the victims by confirming that these acts really occurred. This, of course, cannot take away from the victims all their suffering and bad memories, but he did confirm that they were indeed victims. At the same time, he spared them the suffering that would have been caused had they had to face the accused, come to testify at the proceedings, and evoke again their memories of these events. Mr. Zelenovic agreed to cooperate with this Tribunal fully in any way required by the Prosecution and the Court. Mr. Zelenovic stated that he was aware of the gravity of his crimes, that he accepted responsibility, and that he was awaiting his sentences -- sentencing and that he would accept any sentence handed down by the Chamber. I only wish to point out that the fact that Mr. Zelenovic has accepted responsibility for crimes of this kind, and this is the first time in the history of this Tribunal that somebody has pleaded guilty to rape and all the other circumstances meet to a certain degree the purposes of sentencing. And I think that all the mitigating circumstances and the personal circumstances of the accused should be taken into account when deciding on the sentence. The Defence abides by its proposal that a 7 to 10-year sentence be handed down in full awareness of the gravity of the crimes, but also aware of the fact that this Tribunal has in the past sentenced perpetrators of heinous and cruel crimes, taking any account all the circumstances and handing down sentences which were always much milder when a plea agreement had been reached than they would have been had there been a trial. Thank you, Your Honours. I would conclude on that note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Zelenovic to make a statement, I've got one question to both parties. Reference was made to sentencing before this Tribunal in various cases. Related cases have been referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm referring to Jankovic -- Stankovic, which by now resulted in a judgement. I'm not fully aware on whether these are final judgements, but, at least, would the parties consider it appropriate for this Bench to orient itself in relation to sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia to these judgements as well, because nothing has been said about it. So I would like to know what the position of the parties is in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't address this aspect because, to my knowledge, these are first instance judgements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- who have not yet been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. And also, I don't think we have the judgements already in-house here. So I would be reluctant to say it's comparable, the gravity of the crimes therein are comparable with what this accused did. I can say that with the Kunarac et al. case because we have all judgements. It is notable that for the second -- the most recent judgement against Gojko Jankovic, I think, which was a very high sentence of 35 years, what I could see from the press notes and the homepage of the Bosnia-Herzegovina court he was convicted for murder charges and other charges so it went beyond sexual assault charges only which may make a difference. And also for command responsibility which does not apply to this accused. Now, the other judgement I think contained a sentence of 16 years, and I think it is a more comparable case because it -- it concerns Mr. Stankovic who was also one of the co-perpetrators who was indicted in this first indictment in 1996 which I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I think to know is that there is an English version of the Stankovic judgement. Do I understand you well that you say, "Well, from what I know from Jankovic, it would not be a good idea to orient ourselves on that judgement because it's such a different case, but for Stankovic, if there would be an English version available, it would not be appropriate for Trial Chamber to look at that as well."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that would summarise my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as my learned friend of the Prosecution said, these are judgements that have not become final in terms of Stankovic and Jankovic. The indictment against Gojko Jankovic against the national court of Bosnia-Herzegovina contains far graver charges than defined in these proceedings against Dragan Zelenovic. It's an amended indictment. He's been charged with murder as well, and also in terms of command responsibility. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and I discussed the matter when we were about to conclude the plea agreement. It was then that the Stankovic verdict was passed, 16 years. The Defence is aware of that. But both parties came to the conclusion that we would not highlight that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you have not drawn the attention to it. I mean, that is what I established before. My question was whether you would find it inappropriate if we look at these judgements for our orientation on sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia. And you heard that Ms. Moeller said Jankovic would not be a good idea. Stankovic is different. It comes closer to this case and might therefore assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as the incidents included in this indictment are concerned and also in the Stankovic indictment. From that point of view, yes. But the position of the Defence has been that sentencing practice -- or, rather, the Defence took into account the sentences passed in cases where plea agreements had been reached before this Tribunal, that is to say where circumstances were taken into account such as remorse, admission of guilt and all other circumstances emphasised on the occasions. There are mitigating circumstances presented here presented by the Prosecutor and the Defence. We agree in part on some of these; however, the judgement from the national court of Bosnia and Herzegovina simply does not contain such elements that would make it relevant from this point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jovanovic, if you would orient yourself to other judgement, of course, you would also keep in mind -- you would always keep in mind what is similar and what is different. For example, if we would orient ourselves just assuming that we would we have not decided that yet the Stankovic judgement, of course one of the clear differences is Mr. Stankovic, as far as I'm aware of, did not enter a guilty plea. So therefore that would be one of the obvious differences. But of course the case has other similarities. I'm still not quite clear on your answer. Do you say, No, even Stankovic would be inappropriate or would you say, Look at it, but clearly keep in mind that there are differences apart from similarities?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, Your Honour, there are similarities in respect of the incidents involved and the time period. They pertain to the same time period and what took place in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not an answer to my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- question is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means that judgement can be appraised, but in view of all the circumstances involved in the plea agreement between the Prosecutor and the Defence the result of our talks and agreement was -- rather, the assessment of both parties was that the Trial Chamber would not take into account the practice of the national court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I said, it is not a final judgement, and as far as I know both parties are going to appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the issue on whether or not to look at that judgement. Of course, we could say that it's -- it's published case law and therefore it's -- the Chamber is free to compare whatever judgements, whether final judgements, whether not final yet, to orient itself. I mean, it's just a source of law even if it's not perhaps a definite judgement. The Chamber is seriously considering to at least have a look at the Stankovic judgement, fully aware that it's not final yet, but it's the only thing we have at this moment so much related. If, however, if it might come as a surprise to the parties who -- well, I wouldn't say kept it away from us because if the parties would like for any reason to keep a very short submission and say please be aware that Mr. Stankovic was always yelling in court and was always insulting the judgements so that may have explained -- well, whatever it was, if there's anything you would like to bring to our attention, apart from our assurance that of course if we compare cases for purposes of sentencing, and we'll have to do that in order to strive at the best equality we can provide to accused. So don't think that we just look at so many years but of course we'll have a closer look to it then, but if there's anything, and if this would come as a surprise to you that this would be one of the sources we might take into consideration, reply upon, use as orientation, then you'll have until next week Wednesday to make any brief written submissions. Just in one round. We're not going to start full, new litigation. This is not an encouragement, but at the same time we would not deprive you from the possibility to do that. That is one. Any further documentation on Russia is welcomed. At the same time, Ms. Moeller, I noticed that there was challenge from the Prosecution's side to the statement by Mr. Jovanovic that on from the 22nd or 23rd of August that Mr. Zelenovic spent -- up till the moment when he was transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina he spent uninterruptedly all his time in detention. I notice you didn't challenge that, but any further documentation could give a more solid ground, perhaps, for -- for any finding in this matter. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to know whether it's necessary for me to submit the decision on detention in the original, if the Chamber wishes to assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's no challenge as to the authenticity of the copy that has been provided to the Chamber, so I don't think that that would be necessary. Our concern would be whether this detention order was enforced during the full period of time and whether there was any change in the title on which Mr. Zelenovic was detained. So therefore there's no need to give that to us in the original. Yes? Then, Mr. Zelenovic, we are now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I promised to give you an opportunity to make a brief statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've said everything. Now it is up to you. I will bravely accept any decision that you pass, and I will go through with it. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zelenovic. And when you say, "I've said everything," the Chamber understands that to be a reference to things you earlier said including remorse, including what you expressed in relation to your guilty plea and what this would mean for all, but especially for the victims. Is that well-understood?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I refer to my remorse in respect to the victims and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear to us, Mr. Zelenovic. We -- this concludes this sentencing hearing. The Chamber stands adjourned and will give its Sentencing Judgement in due course.
